p: Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight I shall let you into a secret. It belongs to Mrs Blewitt, my housekeeper, who can add up a grocer's bill in her head before I have found my pencil. I watched her for years before I worked out her method, and when I asked her, she said, "Why, Professor, I just make tens." So tonight, we make tens.
Our road map: the pairs that make ten; adding by making a ten; subtracting by bridging through ten; and a little practice.
## Pairs that make ten
There are only five pairs of whole numbers to learn that add up to ten.

One and nine. Two and eight. Three and seven. Four and six. Five and five. Teachers call these number bonds. I call them friends. If someone says "seven", you should feel the three that is missing, the way you feel the missing step in a dark staircase.
?? A quick test while I pour. What is the friend of six? And the friend of eight?
=> Six's friend is four. Eight's friend is two. Each pair makes ten.
## Making ten when adding
Now the secret. Suppose you must add eight and five. Counting on five ones from eight is slow and easy to muddle. Instead, notice that eight needs two to make ten. So borrow two from the five.
In plain words: eight and two make ten, and there are three left over from the five. Ten and three is thirteen. The trick is that adding to ten is effortless. Anyone can say ten and three.
Let us do another. Seven and six. Seven needs three to make ten. Take three from the six, leaving three.
?? Your turn. Nine and seven. How would you make ten?
=> Nine needs one. Take one from the seven, leaving six. Ten and six is sixteen.
## Bigger numbers, same trick

The trick works just as well with bigger numbers, because of place value. Thirty-eight and five? Thirty-eight needs two to reach forty. Take two from the five, leaving three. Forty and three is forty-three.

Mrs Blewitt does exactly this with pence. A loaf at eighty-seven pence and a pint of milk at forty-five pence. She thinks: eighty-seven needs thirteen to reach a hundred. Take thirteen from forty-five, leaving thirty-two. So the total is one pound thirty-two. By the time the grocer has licked his pencil, she is counting out her coins.
?? A shopping sum, then. Fifty-six pence and twenty-seven pence. Make the fifty-six up to sixty first.
=> Fifty-six needs four to reach sixty. Twenty-seven take away four is twenty-three. Sixty and twenty-three is eighty-three pence.
## Bridging when subtracting
Subtraction works the same way in reverse. To take five from thirteen, first take three to get down to ten, then take the other two.
In plain words: thirteen down to ten uses up three; there are two more to take; ten take away two is eight.

There is another way, which shopkeepers love: counting up. To find thirteen take away five, ask how far it is from five up to thirteen. Five up to ten is five; ten up to thirteen is three more; five and three is eight. This is how change was given in every shop in England. A purchase of sixty-five pence, paid with a pound: sixty-five, seventy, eighty, a pound. Five, ten, twenty: thirty-five pence change.
?? Try counting up. You buy something for seventy-two pence and pay with a pound. What change do you get?
=> From seventy-two up to eighty is eight. From eighty up to a hundred is twenty. Eight and twenty is twenty-eight pence.
## Why this matters

You may wonder why a Professor of Mathematics, who has lectured on the calculus to whole rooms of young men in waistcoats, bothers with making ten. The answer is that every later idea rests on arithmetic you can do without strain. When we reach algebra, I want your mind free to think about the new ideas, not tangled up in seven plus six. Working memory, as your century's psychologists call it, is a small room, and we must not fill it with clutter.
## Summary

The pairs that make ten are one and nine, two and eight, three and seven, four and six, and five and five. To add, make a ten first, and then add what is left. To subtract, bridge down through ten, or count up as shopkeepers do. Next time, we shall add and subtract properly with bigger numbers, column by column, entirely by ear. Until then, my dear friend, practise on your shopping, and give my regards to your grocer.

Good evening, my dear friend. I see you have brought your courage tonight, for we are tackling the times tables, which have caused more tears in English schoolrooms than any other subject except Latin verbs. I mean to dry those tears. The times tables are full of patterns, and patterns are kinder than memorising.
Our road map: what multiplication means; why the order does not matter; the friendly tables of two, four, five, nine and ten; and a few tricks for the stubborn ones.
## Repeated adding
Multiplication is a shortcut for adding the same number again and again. Four times three means four lots of three.
Picture eggs in a box: two rows of six. Two times six is twelve. Or picture the panes in a sash window: three rows of four panes, twelve in all.
## Order does not matter
Here is a gift. Four rows of seven panes, or seven rows of four: turn the window on its side, and it is the same window with the same number of panes.
⟦4\times 7=7\times 4=28⟧

This is the commutative law again, the one we met with adding. It means that once you know four sevens, you know seven fours for free. That halves the work at a stroke. A full table up to ten times ten has a hundred facts, but thanks to this, and the easy ones, only about fifteen are really troublesome.
?? While I pour. If you know that six times eight is forty-eight, what is eight times six?
=> Forty-eight, of course. The order does not matter.
## The friendly tables
The ten times table is the easiest of all, because of place value. Multiplying by ten moves every digit one place to the left. Seven tens are seventy.
The two times table is doubling. Doubling is something the mind does almost by itself. Double eight is sixteen.
The four times table is doubling twice. Four times seven? Double seven is fourteen, double fourteen is twenty-eight.
?? Try it. Four times nine, by doubling twice.
=> Double nine is eighteen. Double eighteen is thirty-six.
The five times table is half of the ten times table. Five times eight? Ten eights would be eighty; five eights is half of that, forty. Five lots is always half of ten lots.
The nine times table is ten lots, minus one lot.

In plain words: ten sevens are seventy; nine sevens are one seven fewer, sixty-three. The nines also have a pretty pattern: the digits of the answer always add up to nine. Eighteen, one and eight. Twenty-seven, two and seven. Thirty-six, forty-five, fifty-four, sixty-three, seventy-two, eighty-one. Each has digits adding to nine. Euclid does not care for this pattern, but then Euclid does not care for anything that is not fish.
## The stubborn ones
What remains? The threes, sixes, sevens and eights, mostly. Here are some handholds.
The six times table is double the threes. Six times seven? Three sevens are twenty-one, and double that is forty-two.
The eight times table is doubling three times. Eight times seven? Double seven, fourteen. Double again, twenty-eight. Double again, fifty-six.
And you can always build from a fact you know. Seven sevens? If you know seven fives are thirty-five, add two more sevens, fourteen. Forty-nine.
⟦7\times 7=7\times 5+7\times 2=35+14=49⟧
?? A stubborn one. Eight times six, by doubling.
=> Eight times six is six doubled three times. Twelve, twenty-four, forty-eight.
## The square numbers

When a number is multiplied by itself, the answer is called a square number, because that many dots can be laid out in a perfect square. One, four, nine, sixteen, twenty-five, thirty-six, forty-nine, sixty-four, eighty-one, a hundred. It is worth knowing these well, for they come back again and again. In algebra and in calculus they will be some of our most loyal companions.
There is a delightful pattern hiding here, too. The gaps between square numbers are the odd numbers. One to four is three. Four to nine is five. Nine to sixteen is seven. And so on, forever.
?? What is the next square number after sixty-four, and what is the gap?
=> Eighty-one. The gap is seventeen, the next odd number after fifteen.
## A word about Victorian schoolrooms

In my day, children chanted their tables in rows, and a mistake might earn a rap on the knuckles. I did not approve then and I do not approve now. Chanting has its place, for rhythm helps memory, but understanding is what lasts. A child who knows that nine sevens is ten sevens minus one will never be lost, even when the chant deserts him.
## Summary

Multiplication is repeated adding. The order does not matter, which halves the work. Use the friendly patterns: tens by moving places, twos by doubling, fours by doubling twice, fives by halving tens, and nines by ten lots minus one. Build stubborn facts from easy ones. Next time we multiply bigger numbers, still entirely by ear. Until then, my dear friend, good night, and may your sevens behave themselves.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight a lecture in praise of being roughly right. Many people think mathematics is all about exact answers. It is not. Much of the time, a good estimate is worth more than a precise answer, because it can be found quickly, in the head, and it tells you whether a precise answer is sensible. An engineer who cannot estimate is a danger to the public. I say this as a man who has crossed a great many Victorian bridges.
Our road map: rounding to easy numbers; estimating sums and products; catching mistakes; and the art of the wild-but-reasoned guess.
## Round, then calculate
To estimate, replace awkward numbers with nearby friendly ones. Forty-nine times twenty-one? Forty-nine is nearly fifty, and twenty-one is nearly twenty. Fifty times twenty is a thousand.
⟦49\times 21\approx 50\times 20=1000⟧
That wavy equals sign means "approximately equal to". The exact answer is one thousand and twenty-nine, so our estimate is very close.
?? While I pour. Estimate three hundred and eighty-seven plus two hundred and nine.
=> Round to four hundred and two hundred: about six hundred. The exact answer is five hundred and ninety-six.
## A trolley of shopping

Mrs Blewitt estimates every shopping basket before she reaches the counter. Two pounds ninety-five, one pound ten, four pounds eighty-nine, sixty pence. She rounds to three, one, five, and a half: nine and a half pounds. The till says nine pounds fifty-four. If the grocer had said fifteen pounds, she would have known at once that something was amiss. Estimating is her shield against error, and occasionally against grocers.
## Catching mistakes

The commonest blunder in arithmetic is a misplaced decimal point or a lost zero. Estimating catches these instantly. Suppose you calculate four point eight times six point one and get two hundred and ninety-two point eight. An estimate says five times six is thirty, so the answer should be near thirty. You have slipped a place. The true answer is twenty-nine point two eight.
?? Someone tells you that one hundred and ninety-eight divided by nine point nine is two hundred. Is that sensible?
=> Estimate: two hundred divided by ten is twenty. So the answer should be about twenty, not two hundred. Someone has slipped a decimal place.
## Overestimate or underestimate?

It can help to know which way your estimate leans. If you round both numbers up, your estimate of a product will be too big. Forty-nine times twenty-one: we rounded forty-nine up and twenty-one down, so the errors partly cancelled, which is why we were so close. When paying a bill, rounding every price up gives a safe overestimate: you will not be embarrassed at the counter.
## The wild but reasoned guess

Now a wonderful game. How many piano tuners are there in London? You cannot possibly know. But you can reason. The physicist Enrico Fermi, born long after my time, made such questions famous, and they are called Fermi problems.

Let us try it for my own day. Suppose London has about five million people, which was roughly so in the eighteen-eighties. Suppose a household is about five people, and one household in twenty has a piano. That gives about a million households, and fifty thousand pianos. Suppose each piano is tuned once a year, and a tuner can tune four pianos a day, working about two hundred and fifty days a year: a thousand pianos a year each. So London needs about fifty piano tuners.

Every step was a guess, but each was a reasonable guess, and errors in different directions tend to cancel. The answer might be off by a factor of two or three, but it will not be off by a factor of a thousand. That is the magic of breaking a big question into small ones.
?? Try a small Fermi problem. Roughly how many hours are there in a year?

=> About three hundred and sixty-five days times twenty-four hours. Round to four hundred times twenty-five, which is ten thousand, a slight overestimate. The true figure is eight thousand seven hundred and sixty. So roughly nine thousand.
## Estimating and confidence

There is a quieter benefit to estimating. When you know roughly what the answer should be, you are no longer at the mercy of the calculation. Fear of mathematics often comes from feeling lost in it, with no idea whether you are right or wrong. An estimate is a lantern. Even in fog, you know which way is home.
## Summary

To estimate, round to friendly numbers, then calculate. Estimates catch big mistakes, especially lost zeros and decimal points. Know whether your estimate leans high or low. And Fermi problems show that even impossible-seeming questions can be answered roughly, by breaking them into reasonable guesses. Next time, rounding properly, with decimal places and significant figures. Until then, my dear friend, be roughly right, and happily so.

Ah, there you are. Come in, mind the cat. Tonight, Arithmetic. It is a reading from Mrs Blewitt's department: reckoning in the head. I have retold it in my own words from the Wikipedia article Arithmetic, written by a great many hands and shared under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licence. The facts are theirs, checked as carefully as I am able; the jokes, I am afraid, are mine.
Tonight, Mrs Blewitt's own subject, and the foundation of everything: arithmetic.
## What it is

Arithmetic, from the Greek word arithmos, number, is the branch of mathematics dealing with numbers and the four operations: addition, subtraction, multiplication and division. Many people add powers and roots to the list. It is the first mathematics we learn, and the one we use every day, at the shop, in the kitchen, and in the counting-house.
## The four operations

Addition combines amounts. Subtraction takes one amount away from another, or finds the difference. Multiplication is repeated addition: four threes are three plus three plus three plus three. Division shares out, or asks how many times one number goes into another. Subtraction undoes addition, and division undoes multiplication.
## The laws

Arithmetic obeys some laws that are so familiar we hardly notice them. The commutative law: order does not matter in adding or multiplying. Two plus three is three plus two. The associative law: grouping does not matter either. Two plus three, then plus four, is two plus, three plus four. And the distributive law: multiplication spreads over addition.
⟦a(b+c)=ab+ac⟧

In plain words: a times, b plus c, equals a b plus a c. Three times, four plus five, is three fours plus three fives, twelve plus fifteen, twenty-seven. This law is what makes long multiplication work, and is the brown-paper parcel being unwrapped.
?? While I pour. Use the distributive law to work out seven times twelve, as seven tens plus seven twos.
=> Seventy plus fourteen: eighty-four.
Subtraction and division, notice, obey neither of the first two laws. Five minus three is not three minus five.
## Order of operations

When several operations appear together, there is an agreed order: brackets first, then powers, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. In British schools, BIDMAS or BODMAS. We spent a whole lecture of the primer on it in a royal kitchen.
## Tools of calculation

People have calculated with fingers, with pebbles, and with the abacus, still used skilfully in parts of Asia. Written methods arrived with the Hindu–Arabic numerals, whose place value turns calculation into simple steps on paper. Napier's logarithms, in 1614, turned multiplication into addition and gave us the slide rule. Mechanical calculators followed, from Pascal's of 1642 to Babbage's engines in my own day, and the electronic computers of your century. Yet the arithmetic inside them is the same as Mrs Blewitt's.
## Arithmetic and number theory

Higher arithmetic, as Gauss called it, is number theory: the study of whole numbers themselves, of primes and divisibility. Gauss called mathematics the queen of the sciences, and number theory the queen of mathematics.
## Summary

Arithmetic deals with numbers and the four operations. It obeys the commutative, associative and distributive laws, follows an agreed order of operations, and has been done with fingers, abacus, paper and machines. Its higher form is number theory.

Addition, usually denoted with the plus sign +, is one of the four basic operations of arithmetic, the other three being subtraction, multiplication, and division. The addition of two whole numbers results in the total or sum of those values combined. For example, the adjacent image shows two columns of apples, one with three apples and the other with two apples, totaling to five apples.

Besides counting items, addition can also be defined and executed without referring to concrete objects, using abstractions called numbers instead, such as integers, real numbers, and complex numbers. Addition belongs to arithmetic, a branch of mathematics. In algebra, another area of mathematics, addition can also be performed on abstract objects such as vectors, matrices, and elements of additive groups.

Addition has several important properties. It is also associative, meaning that when one adds more than two numbers, the order in which addition is performed does not matter. Repeated addition of 1 is the same as counting (see Successor function). Addition of 0 does not change a number. Addition also obeys rules concerning related operations such as subtraction and multiplication.

Performing addition is one of the simplest numerical tasks to perform. Addition of very small numbers is accessible to toddlers; the most basic task, 1 + 1, can be performed by infants as young as five months, and even by some members of other animal species. In primary education, students are taught to add numbers in the decimal system, beginning with single digits and progressively tackling more difficult problems. Mechanical aids range from the ancient abacus to the modern computer, where research on the most efficient implementations of addition continues to this day.
## Notation and terminology

Addition is written using the plus sign "+" between the terms, and the result is expressed with an equals sign. For example, ⟦1 + 2 = 3⟧ reads "one plus two equals three". Nonetheless, there are some situations where addition is understood, even though no symbol appears: a whole number followed immediately by a fraction indicates the sum of the two, called a mixed number, with an example,
$$ 3 \frac{1}{2} = 3 + \frac{1}{2} = \operatorname{3.5.}

In plain words: it says that the two sides are equal. A fraction means the top part divided by the bottom part. It uses a named function, such as sine, cosine or log, which turns one number into another.
This notation can cause confusion, since in most other contexts, juxtaposition denotes multiplication instead.
The numbers or the objects to be added in general addition are collectively referred to as the terms, the addends or the summands. This terminology carries over to the summation of multiple terms.
This is to be distinguished from factors, which are multiplied.

Some authors call the first addend the augend. In fact, during the Renaissance, many authors did not consider the first addend an "addend" at all. Today, due to the commutative property of addition, "augend" is rarely used, and both terms are generally called addends.

All of the above terminology derives from Latin. "Addition" and "add" are English words derived from the Latin verb addere, which is in turn a compound of ad "to" and dare "to give", from the Proto-Indo-European root *deh₃- "to give"; thus to add is to give to. Using the gerundive suffix -nd results in "addend", "thing to be added". Likewise from augere "to increase", one gets "augend", "thing to be increased".

"Sum" and "summand" derive from the Latin noun summa "the highest" or "the top", used in Medieval Latin phrase summa linea ("top line") meaning the sum of a column of numerical quantities, following the ancient Greek and Roman practice of putting the sum at the top of a column.

Addere and summare date back at least to Boethius, if not to earlier Roman writers such as Vitruvius and Frontinus; Boethius also used several other terms for the addition operation. The later Middle English terms "adden" and "adding" were popularized by Chaucer.
## Definition and interpretations

Addition is one of the four basic operations of arithmetic, with the other three being subtraction, multiplication, and division. This operation works by adding two or more terms. An arbitrary number of addition operations is called a summation. An infinite summation is a delicate procedure known as a series, and it can be expressed through capital sigma notation ⟦∑⟧, which compactly denotes iteration of the addition operation based on the given indexes. In plain words: it says that the two sides are equal. A sum, written with the Greek capital sigma, means add up every term as the counter runs from its first value to its last. A power means multiplying a number by itself a given number of times.
Addition is used to model many physical processes. Even for the simple case of adding natural numbers, there are many possible interpretations and even more visual representations.
## Combining sets
Possibly the most basic interpretation of addition lies in combining sets, that is:
When two or more disjoint collections are combined into a single collection, the number of objects in the single collection is the sum of the numbers of objects in the original collections.

This interpretation is easy to visualize, with little danger of ambiguity. It is also useful in higher mathematics (for the rigorous definition it inspires, see § Natural numbers below). However, it is not obvious how one should extend this interpretation to include fractional or negative numbers.

One possibility is to consider collections of objects that can be easily divided, such as pies or, still better, segmented rods. Rather than solely combining collections of segments, rods can be joined end-to-end, which illustrates another conception of addition: adding not the rods but the lengths of the rods.
## Extending a length
A second interpretation of addition comes from extending an initial length by a given length:
When an original length is extended by a given amount, the final length is the sum of the original length and the length of the extension.

The sum ⟦a + b⟧ can be interpreted as a binary operation that combines ⟦a⟧ and ⟦b⟧ algebraically, or it can be interpreted as the addition of ⟦b⟧ more units to ⟦a⟧. Under the latter interpretation, the parts of a sum ⟦a + b⟧ play asymmetric roles, and the operation ⟦a + b⟧ is viewed as applying the unary operation ⟦+ b⟧ to ⟦a⟧. Instead of calling both ⟦a⟧ and ⟦b⟧ addends, it is more appropriate to call ⟦a⟧ the "augend" in this case, since ⟦a⟧ plays a passive role. The unary view is also useful when discussing subtraction, because each unary addition operation has an inverse unary subtraction operation, and vice versa.
## Commutativity
Addition is commutative, meaning that one can change the order of the terms in a sum, but still get the same result. Symbolically, if ⟦a⟧ and ⟦b⟧ are any two numbers, then:
$$ a + b = b + a

The fact that addition is commutative is known as the "commutative law of addition" or "commutative property of addition". Some other binary operations are commutative too as in multiplication, but others are not as in subtraction and division.
## Associativity
Addition is associative, which means that when three or more numbers are added together, the order of operations does not change the result. For any three numbers ⟦a⟧, ⟦b⟧, and ⟦c⟧, it is true that:

When addition is used together with other operations, the order of operations becomes important. In the standard order of operations, addition is a lower priority than exponentiation, nth roots, multiplication and division, but is given equal priority to subtraction.
## Identity element
Adding zero to any number does not change the number. In other words, zero is the identity element for addition, and is also known as the additive identity. In symbols, for every ⟦a⟧, one has:

This law was first identified in Brahmagupta's Brahmasphutasiddhanta in 628 AD, although he wrote it as three separate laws, depending on whether ⟦a⟧ is negative, positive, or zero itself, and he used words rather than algebraic symbols. Later, other Indian mathematicians refined the concept. Around the year 830, Mahavira wrote, "zero becomes the same as what is added to it", corresponding to the unary statement ⟦0 + a = a .⟧ In the 12th century, Bhaskara wrote, "In the addition of [zero], or subtraction of it, the quantity, positive or negative, remains the same", corresponding to the unary statement ⟦a + 0 = a .⟧
## Successor

Within the context of integers, addition of one also plays a special role: for any integer ⟦a⟧, the integer ⟦a + 1⟧ is the least integer greater than ⟦a⟧, also known as the successor of ⟦a⟧. For instance, 3 is the successor of 2, and 7 is the successor of 6. Because of this succession, the value of ⟦a + b⟧ can also be seen as the ⟦b⟧-th successor of ⟦a⟧, making addition an iterated succession. For example, 6 + 2 is 8, because 8 is the successor of 7, which is the successor of 6, making 8 the second successor of 6.

## Units

To numerically add physical quantities with units, they must be expressed with common units. For example, adding 50 milliliters to 150 milliliters gives 200 milliliters. However, if a measure of 5 feet is extended by 2 inches, the sum is 62 inches, since 60 inches is synonymous with 5 feet. On the other hand, it is usually meaningless to try to add 3 meters and 4 square meters, since those units are incomparable; this sort of consideration is fundamental in dimensional analysis.
## Innate ability

Studies on mathematical development starting around the 1980s have exploited the phenomenon of habituation: infants look longer at situations that are unexpected. A seminal experiment by Karen Wynn in 1992 involving Mickey Mouse dolls manipulated behind a screen demonstrated that five-month-old infants expect 1 + 1 to be 2, and they are comparatively surprised when a physical situation seems to imply that 1 + 1 is either 1 or 3. This finding has since been affirmed by a variety of laboratories using different methodologies. Another 1992 experiment with older toddlers, between 18 and 35 months, exploited their development of motor control by allowing them to retrieve ping-pong balls from a box; the youngest responded well for small numbers, while older subjects were able to compute sums up to 5.

Even some nonhuman animals show a limited ability to add, particularly primates. In a 1995 experiment imitating Wynn's 1992 result (but using eggplants instead of dolls), rhesus macaque and cottontop tamarin monkeys performed similarly to human infants. More dramatically, after being taught the meanings of the Arabic numerals 0 through 4, one chimpanzee was able to compute the sum of two numerals without further training. More recently, Asian elephants have demonstrated an ability to perform basic arithmetic.
## Addition by counting

Typically, children first master counting. When given a problem that requires that two items and three items be combined, young children model the situation with physical objects, often fingers or a drawing, and then count the total. As they gain experience, they learn or discover the strategy of "counting-on": asked to find two plus three, children count three past two, saying "three, four, five" (usually ticking off fingers), and arriving at five. This strategy seems almost universal; children can easily pick it up from peers or teachers. Most discover it independently. With additional experience, children learn to add more quickly by exploiting the commutativity of addition by counting up from the larger number, in this case, starting with three and counting "four, five." Eventually children begin to recall certain addition facts ("number bonds"), either through experience or rote memorization. Once some facts are committed to memory, children begin to derive unknown facts from known ones. Such derived facts can be found very quickly and most elementary school students eventually rely on a mixture of memorized and derived facts to add fluently.

Different nations introduce whole numbers and arithmetic at different ages, with many countries teaching addition in pre-school. However, throughout the world, addition is taught by the end of the first year of elementary school.
## Single-digit addition

An ability to add a pair of single digits (numbers from 0 to 9) is a prerequisite for addition of arbitrary numbers in the decimal system. With 10 choices for each of the two digits to be added, this makes 100 single-digit "addition facts", which can be presented in an addition table.

Learning to fluently and accurately compute single-digit additions is a major focus of early schooling in arithmetic. Sometimes students are encouraged to memorize the full addition table by rote, but pattern-based strategies are typically more enlightening and, for most people, more efficient:
Commutative property: Mentioned above, using the pattern ⟦a + b = b + a⟧ reduces the number of "addition facts" from 100 to 55.
One or two more: Adding 1 or 2 is a basic task, and it can be accomplished through counting on or, ultimately, intuition.

Zero: Since zero is the additive identity, adding zero is trivial. Nonetheless, in the teaching of arithmetic, some students are introduced to addition as a process that always increases the addends; word problems may help rationalize the "exception" of zero.
Doubles: Adding a number to itself is related to counting by two and to multiplication. Doubles facts form a backbone for many related facts, and students find them relatively easy to grasp.
A formula is omitted here.
Five and ten: Sums of the form 5 + ⟦x⟧ and 10 + ⟦x⟧ are usually memorized early and can be used for deriving other facts.

As students gain experience with addition, they gradually memorize an increasing number of basic addition facts and become more fluent in recalling them. Repeated practice also helps students recognize relationships among addition facts, allowing them to derive sums that they do not immediately recall. Over time, commonly used facts and strategies such as doubles, near-doubles, making ten, and counting on can become increasingly automatic. This development of fluency allows students to calculate single-digit sums more quickly and accurately, while reducing the amount of deliberate mental effort required for familiar additions.

## Computers

Analog computers work directly with physical quantities, so their addition mechanisms depend on the form of the addends. A mechanical adder might represent two addends as the positions of sliding blocks, in which case they can be added with an averaging lever. If the addends are the rotation speeds of two shafts, they can be added with a differential. A hydraulic adder can add the pressures in two chambers by exploiting Newton's second law to balance forces on an assembly of pistons. The most common situation for a general-purpose analog computer is to add two voltages (referenced to ground); this can be accomplished roughly with a resistor network, but a better design exploits an operational amplifier.
Addition is also fundamental to the operation of digital computers, where the efficiency of addition, in particular the carry mechanism, is an important limitation to overall performance.

The abacus, also called a counting frame, is a calculating tool that was in use centuries before the adoption of the written modern numeral system and is still widely used by merchants, traders and clerks in Asia, Africa, and elsewhere; it dates back to at least 2700–2300 BC, when it was used in Sumer.

Blaise Pascal invented the mechanical calculator in 1642; it was the first operational adding machine. Pascal's calculator was limited by its gravity-assisted carry mechanism, which forced its wheels to only turn one way so it could add. To subtract, the operator had to use the Pascal's calculator's complement, which required as many steps as an addition. Gottfried Leibniz built the stepped reckoner, another mechanical calculator, finished in 1694, and Giovanni Poleni improved on the design in 1709 with a calculating clock made of wood that could perform all four arithmetical operations. These early attempts were not commercially successful but inspired later mechanical calculators of the 19th century.

Adders execute integer addition in electronic digital computers, usually using binary arithmetic. The simplest architecture is the ripple carry adder, which follows the standard multi-digit algorithm. One slight improvement is the carry skip design, again following human intuition; one does not perform all the carries in computing 999 + 1, but one bypasses the group of 9s and skips to the answer.

In practice, computational addition may be achieved via XOR and AND bitwise logical operations in conjunction with bitshift operations. Both XOR and AND gates are straightforward to realize in digital logic, allowing the realization of full adder circuits, which in turn may be combined into more complex logical operations. In modern digital computers, integer addition is typically the fastest arithmetic instruction, yet it has the largest impact on performance since it underlies all floating-point operations as well as such basic tasks as address generation during memory access and fetching instructions during branching. To increase speed, modern designs calculate digits in parallel; these schemes go by such names as carry select, carry lookahead, and the Ling pseudocarry. Many implementations are, in fact, hybrids of these last three designs.
Some decimal computers in the late 1950s and early 1960s used add tables instead of adders, for example RCA 301, IBM 1620.

Arithmetic implemented on a computer can deviate from the mathematical ideal in various ways. For example, if the result of an addition is too large for a computer to store, an arithmetic overflow occurs, resulting in an error message and/or an incorrect answer. Unanticipated arithmetic overflow is a fairly common cause of program errors. Such overflow bugs may be hard to discover and diagnose because they may manifest themselves only for very large input data sets, which are less likely to be used in validation tests. The Year 2000 problem was a series of bugs where overflow errors occurred due to the use of a 2-digit format for years.

Computers have another way of representing numbers, called floating-point arithmetic, which is similar to the scientific notation described above and which reduces the overflow problem. Each floating point number has two parts, an exponent and a mantissa. To add two floating-point numbers, the exponents must match, which typically means shifting the mantissa of the smaller number. If the disparity between the larger and smaller numbers is too great, a loss of precision may result. If many smaller numbers are to be added to a large number, it is best to add the smaller numbers together first and then add the total to the larger number, rather than adding small numbers to the large number one at a time. This makes floating-point addition non-associative in general.

Multiplication is one of the four elementary mathematical operations of arithmetic, with the other ones being addition, subtraction, and division. The result of a multiplication operation is called a product. Multiplication is often denoted by the cross symbol, ×, by the mid-line dot operator, ⋅, by juxtaposition, or, in programming languages, by an asterisk, *.

The multiplication of whole numbers may be thought of as repeated addition; that is, the multiplication of two numbers is equivalent to adding as many copies of one of them, the multiplicand, as the quantity of the other one, the multiplier. Both numbers can be referred to as factors. This is to be distinguished from terms, which are added.
$$ a × b = {b + ⋯ + b}_{a \text{ times}}
In plain words: it says that the two sides are equal. A little number written low, said sub, is a label that tells similar quantities apart.

Whether the first factor is the multiplier or the multiplicand may be ambiguous or depend upon context. For example, the expression ⟦3 × 4⟧ can be phrased as "3 times 4", or "Three groups of four", notating the multiplication symbol with the word of, and evaluated as ⟦4 + 4 + 4⟧, where 3 is the multiplier, but also as "3 multiplied by 4", in which case 3 becomes the multiplicand and is therefore interpreted as ⟦3 + 3 + 3 + 3⟧. One of the main properties of multiplication is the commutative property, which states in this case that adding 3 copies of 4 gives the same result as adding 4 copies of 3. Thus, the designation of multiplier and multiplicand does not affect the result of the multiplication.
Systematic generalizations of this basic definition define the multiplication of integers (including negative numbers), rational numbers (fractions), and real numbers.

Multiplication can also be visualized as counting objects arranged in a rectangle (for whole numbers) or as calculating the area of a rectangle with sides of given lengths. The area of a rectangle remains the same regardless of which side is measured first—a result of the commutative property.

The product of two measurements (or physical quantities) is a new type of measurement (or new quantity), usually with a derived unit of measurement. For example, multiplying the lengths (in meters or feet) of the two sides of a rectangle gives its area (in square meters or square feet). Such a product is the subject of dimensional analysis.

The inverse operation of multiplication is considered division. For example, since 4 multiplied by 3 equals 12, 12 divided by 3 equals 4. Indeed, multiplication by 3, followed by division by 3, yields the original number. The division of a number other than 0 by itself equals 1.

Several mathematical concepts expand upon the fundamental idea of multiplication. The product of a sequence, vector multiplication, complex numbers, and matrices are all examples where this can be seen. These more advanced constructs tend to affect the basic properties in their own ways, such as becoming noncommutative in matrices and some forms of vector multiplication or changing the sign of complex numbers.
## Notation
In arithmetic, multiplication is often written using the multiplication sign (either × or ⟦×⟧) between the factors (that is, in infix notation). For example,

⟦2 × 3 = 6 ,⟧ ("two times three equals six"); ⟦3 × 4 = 12 ,⟧; ⟦2 × 3 × 5 = 6 × 5 = 30 ,⟧; ⟦2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32.⟧; The cross sign was first used by Edward Wright in 1618; There are other mathematical notations for multiplication.

Multiplication is also denoted by a middle-position dot: ⟦5 ⋅ 2⟧. Middle dot was first used by G. W. Leibniz in 1698, because the multiplication sign × is easily confused with the common mathematical variable ⟦x⟧. The middle dot notation, or dot operator, is now standard in the United States and other countries. When the dot operator character is not accessible, the interpunct (·) is used. In most European and other countries that use a comma as a decimal point (and a period as a thousands separator), the multiplication sign or a middle dot is used to indicate multiplication. Historically, in the United Kingdom and Ireland, the middle dot was sometimes used for the decimal point to prevent it from disappearing in the ruled line, and the full stop (period) was used for multiplication. However, since the Ministry of Technology ruled in 1968 that the period be used as the decimal point, and the International System of Units (SI) standard has since been widely adopted, this usage is now found only in the more traditional journals such as The Lancet.

In algebra, multiplication involving variables is often written as a juxtaposition (for example ⟦x y⟧ for ⟦x⟧ times ⟦y⟧ or ⟦5 x⟧ for five times ⟦x⟧), also called implied multiplication. In computer programming, the asterisk (as in 5*2) is still the most common notation. The numbers to be multiplied are generally called the factors (as in factorization). The number to be multiplied is the multiplicand, and the number by which it is multiplied is the multiplier. ## Multiplication in group theory

There are many sets that, under the operation of multiplication, satisfy the axioms that define group structure. These axioms are closure, associativity, and the inclusion of an identity element and inverses.

A simple example is the set of non-zero rational numbers. Here the identity element is 1, as opposed to groups under addition where the identity is typically 0. Note that with the rationals, zero must be excluded because, under multiplication, it does not have an inverse: there is no rational number that can be multiplied by zero to result in 1. In this example, the result is an abelian group, but that is not always the case.

To see this, consider the set of invertible square matrices of a given dimension over a given field. Here, it is straightforward to verify closure, associativity, and inclusion of identity (the identity matrix) and inverses. However, matrix multiplication is not commutative, which shows that this group is non-abelian.

Another fact worth noticing is that the integers under multiplication do not form a group—even if zero is excluded. This is easily seen by the nonexistence of an inverse for all elements other than 1 and minus 1.

Division is one of the four basic operations of arithmetic. The other operations are addition, subtraction, and multiplication. What is being divided is called the dividend, which is divided by the divisor, and the result is called the quotient.

At an elementary level the division of two natural numbers is, among other possible interpretations, the process of calculating the number of times one number is contained within another. For example, if 20 apples are divided evenly between 4 people, everyone receives 5 apples (see picture).

The division with remainder or Euclidean division of two natural numbers provides an integer quotient, which is the number of times the second number is completely contained in the first number, and a remainder, which is the part of the first number that remains, when in the course of computing the quotient, no further full chunk of the size of the second number can be allocated. For example, if 21 apples are divided between 4 people, everyone receives 5 apples, and 1 apple remains.

For division to always yield one number rather than a quotient and a remainder, the natural numbers must be extended to rational numbers or real numbers. In these enlarged number systems, division is the inverse operation to multiplication, that is ⟦a = c / b⟧ means ⟦a × b = c⟧, as long as ⟦b⟧ is not zero; division by zero is not defined. In the 21-apples example, everyone would receive 5 apples and a quarter of an apple, with none left over.

Both forms of division appear in various algebraic structures, different ways of defining mathematical structure. Those in which a Euclidean division (with remainder) is defined are called Euclidean domains and include polynomial rings in one indeterminate (which define multiplication and addition over single-variabled formulas). Those in which a division (with a single result) by all nonzero elements is defined are called fields and division rings. In a ring the elements by which division is always possible are called the units (for example, 1 and minus 1 in the ring of integers). Another generalization of division to algebraic structures is the quotient group, in which the result of "division" is a group rather than a number.
## Introduction

The simplest way of viewing division is in terms of quotition and partition: from the quotition perspective, ⟦20 / 5⟧ means the number of 5s that must be added to get 20. In terms of partition, ⟦20 / 5⟧ means the size of each of 5 parts into which a set of size 20 is divided. For example, 20 apples divide into five groups of four apples, meaning that "twenty divided by five is equal to four". This is denoted as ⟦20 / 5 = 4⟧, or a long formula. In the example, 20 is the dividend, 5 is the divisor, and 4 is the quotient.

Unlike the other basic operations, when dividing natural numbers there is sometimes a remainder that will not go evenly into the dividend. For example, ⟦10 / 3⟧ leaves a remainder of 1, as 10 is not a multiple of 3. Sometimes this remainder is added to the quotient as a fractional part, so ⟦10 / 3⟧ is equal to ⟦⁠3+1/3⁠⟧ or ⟦3.33...⟧, but in the context of integer division, where numbers have no fractional part, the remainder is kept separately (or exceptionally, discarded or rounded). When the remainder is kept as a fraction, it leads to a rational number. The set of all rational numbers is created by extending the integers with all possible results of divisions of integers.

Unlike multiplication and addition, division is not commutative, meaning that ⟦a / b⟧ is not always equal to ⟦b / a⟧. Division is also not, in general, associative, meaning that when dividing multiple times, the order of division can change the result. For example, ⟦(24 / 6) / 2 = 2⟧, but ⟦24 / (6 / 2) = 8⟧ (where the use of parentheses indicates that the operations inside parentheses are performed before the operations outside parentheses).
Division is traditionally considered as left-associative. That is, if there are multiple divisions in a row, the order of calculation goes from left to right:
Division is right-distributive over addition and subtraction, in the sense that
$$ \frac{a ± b}{c} = ( a ± b ) / c = ( a / c ) ± ( b / c ) = \frac{a}{c} ± \frac{b}{c}
In plain words: it says that the two sides are equal. A fraction means the top part divided by the bottom part.
This is the same for multiplication, as ⟦( a + b ) × c = a × c + b × c⟧. However, division is not left-distributive, as
$$ \frac{a}{b + c} = a / ( b + c ) ≠ ( a / b ) + ( a / c ) = \frac{a c + a b}{b c}
This is unlike the case in multiplication, which is both left-distributive and right-distributive, and thus distributive.

## Manual methods

Division is often introduced through the notion of "sharing out" a set of objects, for example a pile of lollies, into a number of equal portions. Distributing the objects several at a time in each round of sharing to each portion leads to the idea of 'chunking' – a form of division where one repeatedly subtracts multiples of the divisor from the dividend itself.
By allowing one to subtract more multiples than what the partial remainder allows at a given stage, more flexible methods, such as the bidirectional variant of chunking, can be developed as well.

More systematically and more efficiently, two integers can be divided with pencil and paper with the method of short division, if the divisor is small, or long division, if the divisor is larger. If the dividend has a fractional part (expressed as a decimal fraction), one can continue the procedure past the ones place as far as desired. If the divisor has a fractional part, one can restate the problem by moving the decimal to the right in both numbers until the divisor has no fraction, which can make the problem easier to solve (for example 10/2.5 = 100/25 = 4).
Division can be calculated with an abacus.
Logarithm tables can be used to divide two numbers, by subtracting the two numbers' logarithms, then looking up the antilogarithm of the result.

Division can be calculated with a slide rule by aligning the divisor on the C scale with the dividend on the D scale. The quotient can be found on the D scale where it is aligned with the left index on the C scale. The user is responsible, however, for mentally keeping track of the decimal point.

Give the answer as a fraction representing a rational number, so the result of the division of 26 by 11 is ⟦\frac{26}{11}⟧ (or as a mixed number, so ⟦\frac{26}{11} = 2 \frac{4}{11} .⟧) Usually the resulting fraction should be simplified: the result of the division of 52 by 22 is also ⟦\frac{26}{11}⟧. This simplification may be done by factoring out the greatest common divisor.

Give the answer as an integer quotient and a remainder, so ⟦\frac{26}{11} = 2 \text{ remainder } 4.⟧ To make the distinction with the previous case, this division, with two integers as result, is sometimes called Euclidean division, because it is the basis of the Euclidean algorithm.
Give the integer quotient as the answer, so ⟦\frac{26}{11} = 2.⟧ This is the floor function applied to case 2 or 3. It is sometimes called integer division, and denoted by "//".

Dividing integers in a computer program requires special care. Some programming languages treat integer division as in case 5 above, so the answer is an integer. Other languages, such as MATLAB and every computer algebra system return a rational number as the answer, as in case 3 above. These languages also provide functions to get the results of the other cases, either directly or from the result of case 3.

Names and symbols used for integer division include div, /, and \. Definitions vary regarding integer division when the dividend or the divisor is negative: rounding may be toward zero (so called T-division) or toward −infinity (F-division); rarer styles can occur – see modulo operation for the details.
Divisibility rules can sometimes be used to quickly determine whether one integer divides exactly into another.
## Of rational numbers
The result of dividing two rational numbers is another rational number when the divisor is not 0. The division of two rational numbers p/q and r/s can be computed as
$$ \frac{p / q}{r / s} = \frac{p}{q} × \frac{s}{r} = \frac{p s}{q r}
All four quantities are integers, and only p may be 0. This definition ensures that division is the inverse operation of multiplication.
## Of real numbers
A formula is omitted here.
## Of complex numbers
Dividing two complex numbers (when the divisor is nonzero) results in another complex number, which is found using the conjugate of the denominator:

$$ \frac{p + i q}{r + i s} = \frac{( p + i q ) ( r − i s )}{( r + i s ) ( r − i s )} = \frac{p r + q s + i ( q r − p s )}{r^{2} + s^{2}} = \frac{p r + q s}{r^{2} + s^{2}} + i \frac{q r − p s}{r^{2} + s^{2}}
In plain words: it says that the two sides are equal. A power means multiplying a number by itself a given number of times.
Division for complex numbers expressed in polar form is simpler than the definition above:
$$ \frac{p e^{i q}}{r e^{i s}} = \frac{p e^{i q} e^{− i s}}{r e^{i s} e^{− i s}} = \frac{p}{r} e^{i ( q − s )}
A formula is omitted here.
## Of polynomials

One can define the division operation for polynomials in one variable over a field. Then, as in the case of integers, one has a remainder. See Euclidean division of polynomials, and, for hand-written computation, polynomial long division or synthetic division.
## Of matrices

One can define a division operation for matrices. The usual way to do this is to define A / B = AB, where ⟦B^{-1}⟧ denotes the inverse of B, but it is far more common to write out AB explicitly to avoid confusion. An elementwise division can also be defined in terms of the Hadamard product.
## Left and right division

Because matrix multiplication is not commutative, one can also define a left division or so-called backslash-division as ⟦A \ B = A^{-1}B⟧. For this to be well defined, ⟦B^{-1}⟧ need not exist, however ⟦A^{-1}⟧ does need to exist. To avoid confusion, division as defined by ⟦A / B = AB^{-1}⟧ is sometimes called right division or slash-division in this context.

With left and right division defined this way, ⟦A / (BC)⟧ is in general not the same as ⟦(A / B) / C⟧, nor is ⟦(AB) \ C⟧ the same as ⟦A \ (B \ C)⟧. However, it holds that ⟦A / (BC) = (A / C) / B⟧ and ⟦(AB) \ C = B \ (A \ C)⟧.
## Pseudoinverse

To avoid problems when ⟦A^{-1}⟧ and/or ⟦B^{-1}⟧ do not exist, division can also be defined as multiplication by the pseudoinverse. That is, ⟦A / B = AB^{+}⟧ and ⟦A \ B = A^{+}B⟧, where ⟦A^{+}⟧ and ⟦B^{+}⟧ denote the pseudoinverses of ⟦A⟧ and ⟦B⟧.
## Abstract algebra

In abstract algebra, given a magma with binary operation ∗ (which could nominally be termed multiplication), left division of b by a (written ⟦a \ b⟧) is typically defined as the solution x to the equation ⟦a ∗ x = b⟧, if this exists and is unique. Similarly, right division of b by a (written ⟦b / a⟧) is the solution y to the equation ⟦y ∗ a = b⟧. Division in this sense does not require ∗ to have any particular properties (such as commutativity, associativity, or an identity element). A magma for which both ⟦a \ b⟧ and ⟦b / a⟧ exist and are unique for all a and all b (the Latin square property) is a quasigroup. In a quasigroup, division in this sense is always possible, even without an identity element and hence without inverses.

"Division" in the sense of "cancellation" can be done in any magma by an element with the cancellation property. Examples include matrix algebras, quaternion algebras, and quasigroups. In an integral domain, where not every element need have an inverse, division by a cancellative element a can still be performed on elements of the form ab or ca by left or right cancellation, respectively. If a ring is finite and every nonzero element is cancellative, then by an application of the pigeonhole principle, every nonzero element of the ring is invertible, and division by any nonzero element is possible. To learn about when algebras (in the technical sense) have a division operation, refer to the page on division algebras. In particular Bott periodicity can be used to show that any real normed division algebra must be isomorphic to either the real numbers R, the complex numbers C, the quaternions H, or the octonions O.

Division of any number by zero in most mathematical systems is undefined, because zero multiplied by any finite number always results in the product being zero. Entry of such an expression into most calculators produces an error message. However, in certain mathematical structures, division by zero is possible, such as in the zero ring and in algebraic structures such as wheels. In these structures, the meaning of division is different from that of traditional definitions.

Draw your chair nearer the fire. Our subject this evening is Multiplication table. It is a reading from Mrs Blewitt's department: reckoning in the head. I have retold it in my own words from the Wikipedia article Multiplication table, written by a great many hands and shared under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licence. The facts are theirs, checked as carefully as I am able; the jokes, I am afraid, are mine.

Tonight, the times tables. Many of us remember chanting them in a classroom, with a master at the front and a cane on the desk. I promise there is no cane here, and Euclid, who cannot multiply, is entirely unbothered.
## What it is

A multiplication table is a grid. Write the numbers along the top and down the side; where a row and a column meet, write their product. So where the row for six meets the column for seven, you find forty-two. Schoolchildren have learned such tables by heart for many centuries.
## Very old tables

The oldest known decimal multiplication table was found on bamboo strips from China, dated to about three hundred and five years before Christ, now known as the Tsinghua bamboo slips. Babylonian scribes had multiplication tables too, in base sixty, on clay. In Europe, the table is often called the table of Pythagoras, though there is no good evidence that Pythagoras made it.
## Up to twelve

Why do British children learn up to twelve times twelve, and not just ten times ten? Because of our old money and measures. There were twelve pence in a shilling and twelve inches in a foot, and a dozen and a gross, twelve twelves, were standard quantities. Mrs Blewitt, who learned her tables up to twelve, maintains that anyone who stops at ten is a foreigner or a scoundrel.
## Halving the work

The table is symmetrical. Six sevens and seven sixes are both forty-two, because multiplication does not care about order. So once you know one half of the table, you know the other. And the ones and tens columns are free. That leaves surprisingly few facts to memorise.
?? While I pour. If you know three eights is twenty-four, what is eight threes?
=> Twenty-four. Order does not matter in multiplication.
## Patterns

The table hides patterns. In the nines, the digits of each product add to nine: eighteen, twenty-seven, thirty-six, and so on, and the tens digit is one less than the number you multiplied by. The squares lie along the diagonal. Each square is one more than the product of its neighbours: seven sevens is forty-nine, while six eights is forty-eight. That pattern, as you heard in the algebra lectures, is really a difference of two squares.
?? Check: five fives, and four sixes.
=> Twenty-five and twenty-four. One apart, as promised.
## Summary

A multiplication table lists products in a grid. The oldest decimal one is Chinese, from about 305 BC. British tables run to twelve because of pence, inches and dozens. Symmetry halves the work, and patterns such as the nines and the squares make the rest easier.

Ah, there you are. Come in, mind the cat. Tonight, Mental calculation. It is a reading from Mrs Blewitt's department: reckoning in the head. I have retold it in my own words from the Wikipedia article Mental calculation, written by a great many hands and shared under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licence. The facts are theirs, checked as carefully as I am able; the jokes, I am afraid, are mine.

Tonight, Mrs Blewitt's department proper: reckoning in the head. She has asked me to say that she is not a party to any of the shortcuts below, as she does it all instinctively. I record her statement without comment.
## Why in the head

Mental calculation means arithmetic without pencil, paper, or machine. It is useful at the shop, essential for estimating, and rather good exercise for the mind. And for a listener without a page, it is the natural way to calculate.
## Rounding and compensating

Round a number to something friendly, calculate, then correct. Ninety-nine times seven: a hundred sevens is seven hundred; we used one seven too many, so take away seven, six hundred and ninety-three. Two hundred and forty-eight plus three hundred and ninety-nine: add four hundred, six hundred and forty-eight, then take one away, six hundred and forty-seven.
?? While I pour. What is forty-nine times six?
=> Fifty sixes is three hundred; take away one six: two hundred and ninety-four.
## Splitting
Break numbers into parts. Thirty-six times four: thirty times four is a hundred and twenty, six times four is twenty-four, together a hundred and forty-four.
## Doubling and halving

Halve one number and double the other, and the product is unchanged. Sixteen times twenty-five becomes eight times fifty, becomes four times a hundred: four hundred. Multiplying by five is multiplying by ten and halving.
?? Use halving and doubling: what is fourteen times fifteen?
=> Seven times thirty, two hundred and ten.
## Squaring numbers that end in five

To square a number ending in five, take the tens digit, multiply it by one more than itself, and put twenty-five after it. Thirty-five squared: three times four is twelve, then twenty-five: one thousand two hundred and twenty-five.
## The great calculators

Some people have had astonishing powers. In my own century, Zerah Colburn, an American boy, toured Britain performing feats of calculation; and George Parker Bidder, the son of a Devon stonemason, was exhibited as the Calculating Boy, before becoming a distinguished railway engineer. In the twentieth century, Shakuntala Devi of India multiplied two thirteen-digit numbers in her head in 1980, a feat recorded by Guinness. Today there are competitions, such as the Mental Calculation World Cup. Most of these champions use learned techniques and long practice, not magic.
## Summary

Mental calculation uses shortcuts: round and compensate, split numbers into parts, double and halve, and special tricks such as squaring numbers ending in five. Great calculators like Bidder and Shakuntala Devi show how far practice can go.

Settle back, my friend, and let me tell you about Estimation. It is a reading from Mrs Blewitt's department: reckoning in the head. I have retold it in my own words from the Wikipedia article Estimation, written by a great many hands and shared under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licence. The facts are theirs, checked as carefully as I am able; the jokes, I am afraid, are mine.
Tonight, the gentle art of being roughly right, which, as Mrs Blewitt says, is a great deal more useful than being precisely wrong.
## What estimation is

To estimate is to find a value that is close enough for some purpose, when the exact value is unknown, uncertain, or simply not worth the trouble. How much will the groceries cost? About two pounds. How long to walk to St Paul's? About half an hour. An estimate is not a guess thrown at a wall; it is reasoning with rounded numbers.
## Rounding

The simplest method is rounding: replace awkward numbers with nearby friendly ones, then calculate. Forty-nine times twenty-one is about fifty times twenty, a thousand. The exact answer is one thousand and twenty-nine, and the estimate is within three per cent.
?? While I pour. Estimate three hundred and ninety-eight times five.
=> About four hundred times five, two thousand. The exact answer is one thousand nine hundred and ninety.
## Fermi problems

The Italian-American physicist Enrico Fermi, who worked on the first nuclear reactor, was famous for estimating things in his head by breaking them into parts. The classic example, often used in teaching, is: how many piano tuners are there in Chicago? You estimate the population, the share of households with a piano, how often a piano is tuned, and how many pianos a tuner can manage in a year. Each guess may be rough, but the errors tend to partly cancel, and the answer is often within a factor of two or three of the truth. Such questions are now called Fermi problems. The story goes that at the first atomic test in 1945, Fermi estimated the strength of the blast by dropping scraps of paper and seeing how far the blast wave carried them; his estimate was of the right order.
## Estimation in statistics

In statistics, an estimate has a more technical meaning: a value calculated from a sample to stand for a value in a whole population. If a hundred people chosen at random include thirty who take sugar in their tea, we estimate that about thirty per cent of all people do. Statisticians attach a margin of error to say how far off such an estimate might be.
## Checking

Estimation is also the best guard against blunders. Before trusting a calculation, ask whether it is roughly the size you expected. If a calculation says a cup of tea holds fifty litres, a decimal point has gone astray. Many a bridge has been saved by an engineer who asked, does this look about right?
?? A lecture lasts twenty minutes and I say about a hundred and fifty words a minute. Roughly how many words is that?
=> About three thousand.
## Summary

Estimation finds values close enough for a purpose, using rounded numbers. Fermi problems break a question into parts that can be roughly guessed. In statistics, an estimate stands for a population value calculated from a sample. And estimation is the best check on any calculation.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight's lecture is on Order of magnitude. It is a reading from Mrs Blewitt's department: reckoning in the head. I have retold it in my own words from the Wikipedia article Order of magnitude, written by a great many hands and shared under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licence. The facts are theirs, checked as carefully as I am able; the jokes, I am afraid, are mine.
Tonight, a short lecture on thinking big, and small, in tens.
## Powers of ten

An order of magnitude is a factor of ten. To say that one thing is an order of magnitude larger than another is to say it is roughly ten times larger. Two orders of magnitude means about a hundred times; three, about a thousand times. The phrase lets us compare quantities that are wildly different in size without fussing over details.
## Finding the order

The order of magnitude of a number is, roughly, its power of ten when written in standard form, which we met at base camp. Three thousand is three times ten to the three, so its order of magnitude is three. Four hundred thousand is four times ten to the five: order five. A thousandth is ten to the minus three. Roughly speaking, for a whole number, it is one less than the number of digits.
?? While I pour. What is the order of magnitude of seventy thousand?
=> Seven times ten to the four: order four.
## Rounding to orders

There is a small subtlety: when should we round up to the next power of ten? Five is halfway between one and ten when counting, but on a scale of multiplying, the halfway point between one and ten is the square root of ten, about three point one six. So some people say that four hundred is closer, in order of magnitude, to a thousand than to a hundred. I shall not insist on it at the dinner table.
## Thinking in orders

Physicists love orders of magnitude. A human hair is about a tenth of a millimetre across. A person is about a metre or two tall. The Earth is about ten million metres across. The distance to the Sun is about a hundred and fifty billion metres. Placing things on such a ladder of tens gives a feeling for the size of the world that exact figures cannot.
?? Roughly how many orders of magnitude separate a metre-high child from the Earth, ten million metres across?
=> Seven: ten million is ten to the seven.
## Scales built on orders

Several familiar scales count in orders of magnitude. The decibel scale for loudness, the Richter scale for earthquakes, and the pH scale for acidity are logarithmic: each step up means a multiplication, not an addition. An earthquake of magnitude six releases far more energy than one of five, not merely a little more. Logarithms, as you heard on the ridge, are the mathematics of orders of magnitude.
## Summary

An order of magnitude is a factor of ten. The order of a number is its power of ten in standard form. Physicists use orders to grasp the scale of things, and scales such as decibels and the Richter scale count in them.

Draw your chair nearer the fire. Our subject this evening is Casting out nines. It is a reading from Mrs Blewitt's department: reckoning in the head. I have retold it in my own words from the Wikipedia article Casting out nines, written by a great many hands and shared under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licence. The facts are theirs, checked as carefully as I am able; the jokes, I am afraid, are mine.
Tonight, a trick that bookkeepers used for centuries to check their sums. Mrs Blewitt swears by it, and she has caught the grocer more than once.
## Digit sums

Take any whole number and add its digits. If the result has more than one digit, add those, and so on until you have one digit. Treat nine as nought. What you get is the remainder when the number is divided by nine. For example, three hundred and fifty-eight: three plus five plus eight is sixteen; one plus six is seven. And indeed three hundred and fifty-eight is thirty-nine nines and seven over. Getting rid of the nines in this way is called casting out nines.
?? While I pour. What does casting out nines give for one thousand two hundred and thirty-four?
=> One plus two plus three plus four is ten, and one plus nought is one.
## Why it works

Ten is nine plus one. So a hundred, ten tens, is one more than a multiple of nine, and so is a thousand. Each digit is therefore worth itself, plus some multiple of nine, wherever it stands. Throw away the nines, and only the digits remain.
## Checking a sum

Now the trick. To check an addition, cast out nines from each number added, add those results, and cast out nines again. Do the same for the answer. The two must match. The same works for subtraction and for multiplication: multiply the remainders and compare with the remainder of the answer.

Let us check: twenty-three times forty-five equals one thousand and thirty-five. Twenty-three gives five. Forty-five gives nine, which is nought. Five times nought is nought. One thousand and thirty-five: one plus nought plus three plus five, nine, which is nought. They match. Good.
?? Check this claimed sum: three hundred and twelve plus one hundred and seventy-five equals four hundred and ninety-seven.

=> Three hundred and twelve gives six; one hundred and seventy-five gives thirteen, so four. Six plus four is ten, so one. Four hundred and ninety-seven gives twenty, so two. They do not match: the sum is wrong. The true answer is four hundred and eighty-seven.
## Its limits

If the check fails, the calculation is certainly wrong. If it passes, the calculation is probably right, but not certainly. Swapping two digits, writing fifty-four for forty-five, does not change the digit sum, so the check cannot see it. Nor can it see an error of exactly nine, or a misplaced decimal point.
## History

The method was known to Indian and Arabic mathematicians, and was described in Europe by Fibonacci in Liber Abaci. It was taught to clerks and schoolchildren for centuries, until calculating machines made it rarer. I still use it when the butcher's bill looks suspicious.
## Summary

Casting out nines replaces a number by its digit sum, the remainder after dividing by nine. It checks additions, subtractions and multiplications: a mismatch proves an error; a match makes the answer likely but not certain, since swapped digits slip through. It came to Europe through Fibonacci.

Settle back, my friend, and let me tell you about Number sense. It is a reading from Mrs Blewitt's department: reckoning in the head. I have retold it in my own words from the Wikipedia article Number sense, written by a great many hands and shared under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licence. The facts are theirs, checked as carefully as I am able; the jokes, I am afraid, are mine.
Tonight a short lecture on something every good teacher prizes and no examination quite measures: number sense.
## What it is

Number sense is a feel for numbers. It means knowing roughly how big a number is, how numbers relate to one another, and what happens when they are combined. Someone with good number sense knows, without calculating, that forty-nine times fifty-one is close to two thousand five hundred, that half of a big number is still big, and that dividing by a half makes a number larger.
?? While I pour. Without working it out exactly, is three hundred and ninety-eight plus four hundred and five more or less than eight hundred?
=> More. Three hundred and ninety-eight is two less than four hundred, and four hundred and five is five more, so the total is three more than eight hundred.
## Born with it

Psychologists find that number sense begins early. Infants a few months old notice when a small collection changes from two to three objects. Many animals, from chimpanzees to crows to fish, can tell small quantities apart, and roughly compare larger ones. The French researcher Stanislas Dehaene has argued that we inherit an approximate number sense, which schooling then sharpens and extends with words and symbols.
## Building it

Teachers build number sense by encouraging mental arithmetic, estimation, and many ways of looking at the same number: twenty-four as two twelves, as three eights, as twenty and four. It is why I keep asking you to estimate before calculating, and why Mrs Blewitt, who has number sense in abundance, can tell from across the shop that a bill is wrong before she has added it.
## Why it matters

Number sense is linked with later success in mathematics, and its absence is one reason some people feel lost. The good news, which I learned at the Mechanics' Institute, is that it can be grown at any age. It needs only patience and practice, and a teacher who does not hurry.
## Summary

Number sense is a feel for the sizes and relations of numbers. Infants and animals show an inborn version of it, which schooling extends. It grows through estimation, mental arithmetic and seeing numbers in many ways, and it can be developed at any age.
